strengths: Well-motivated approach addressing the practical bottleneck of computational cost in diffusion-based RL; MeanFlow's few-step capability is sensible and effective
Technical solutions are sound: average divergence network elegantly mirrors MeanFlow concepts for likelihood estimation; ESS-weighted SNIS estimator is principled and theoretically grounded

Comprehensive experimental validation across 14 environments with extensive ablations demonstrating necessity of each component; strong empirical results showing 50% training time reduction with maintained performance
Clear presentation with detailed algorithms, hyperparameter tables, and supporting analysis in appendices; reproducibility well-supported with implementation details
Convergence analysis provided (Propositions B.1-B.2) with bias-variance decomposition of proposed estimators documented in appendices
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: MeanFlow models are from concurrent work (Geng et al. 2025); average divergence network is straightforward extension; relies on standard SNIS techniques with ESS weighting—overall feels more like engineering than fundamental research advance

Theory-practice gap: Proposition B.2 assumes K₁, K₂ → ∞ and Boltzmann policy in class Π, but finite samples and incomplete optimization used in practice with no empirical verification these assumptions hold; impact of function approximation errors unanalyzed

Expressivity assumption never validated empirically: Proposition B.2 critically requires π*(·|s) ∈ Π but paper provides no characterization of when this holds or how to verify it; behavior when assumption fails is unexplored

Incomplete efficiency analysis: Inference latency still 3× higher than one-step policies (0.46 ms vs 0.15 ms); action selection overhead at inference (M=10 candidates) not fully accounted for in reported efficiency metrics; real-time control applications less practical than claimed

Limited failure mode analysis: ADN approximation error shows 10-20% relative error (Fig. 6c) but impact on policy learning unclear; no characterization of when SNIS estimators become unreliable or detailed analysis of why MFPO succeeds where DIME fails with few steps

Theory-practice mismatches unquantified: Action likelihood approximation via average divergence (Eq. 18) lacks error analysis; policy improvement objective (Eq. 28) differs from true KL minimization (Eq. 4) when Boltzmann outside policy class, but practical impact unclear

Modest experimental scope: Only continuous control with 8-27D action spaces tested; scalability to high-dimensional actions unverified; no visual observations or other modalities; comparisons limited to diffusion baselines and SAC/TD3, missing recent efficient RL methods

Hyperparameter complexity: Multiple hyperparameters (α, K₁, K₂, N, T) require tuning; while ablations provided on single environment, generalization to diverse task structures not thoroughly explored; ρ = 0.5 claimed robust but limited justification

strengths: Addresses a genuine practical bottleneck in diffusion-based RL by achieving 50% training time reduction with only 2 sampling steps
Sound technical engineering in adapting MeanFlow theory to RL through the Average Divergence Network and principled AIVE with ESS-weighted SNIS
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 14 tasks with detailed ablations, hyperparameter analysis, and supplementary experiments
Well-motivated problem and clear presentation of technical approach despite complexity
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: primarily applies an existing concurrent method (MeanFlow, Geng et al. 2025) to RL using standard soft policy iteration; ADN is a straightforward adaptation and AIVE merely applies existing SNIS techniques with ESS weighting

Critical experimental fairness issues: baseline methods (DIME, MaxEntDP, DACER) are designed and optimized for 16-20 steps but evaluated at 2 steps; Figure 4 suggests DIME's looseness reflects its particular entropy bound rather than fundamental expressivity limits; proper comparison requires re-tuning all methods for 2-step operation

Overclaimed results: timing comparisons use JAX implementations across different frameworks; inference timing excludes the required M=10 action candidate generations; performance differences in Figures 2, 7, 8 are mixed and often within noise, yet framing suggests consistent superiority

Weak theoretical guarantees: convergence analysis assumes K₁, K₂ → ∞ but uses K₁=16, K₂=32; claims policy class is sufficiently expressive to represent π* without verification; assumes solutions to Eq. (28) and (4) are close without justification

Heavy reliance on unvalidated foundation: MeanFlow models are very recent (Geng et al. 2025) and not yet empirically established in RL; Table 1 compares 2-step MeanFlow against 16-20-step diffusion rather than other 2-step methods

Technical concerns with ADN: recursive training target with stop-gradient breaks true divergence computation; Figure 6(c) shows 0.1-0.4 relative error throughout training with no sensitivity analysis on how this propagates through policy improvement; only compared against 1000-step Euler approximation, not ground truth

Missing key comparisons: no systematic evaluation against other few-step acceleration methods (consistency models, DPM-Solver++, shortcut models); limited to small action spaces and continuous control without image-based tasks

Limited scope and generalization: no offline RL evaluation; hyperparameter ρ=0.5 claimed task-independent but set per-task; action selection with M=10 candidates is unshared design choice not compared with baselines

strengths: Well-motivated practical contribution: Addresses genuine computational bottleneck of diffusion-based RL (10-20 steps → 2 steps), achieving ~50% training time reduction with comparable performance

Principled technical solutions: Average Divergence Network (ADN) elegantly adapts MeanFlow's average velocity concept to intractable divergence integral; Adaptive Instantaneous Velocity Estimation (AIVE) thoughtfully combines dual SNIS proposals with ESS weighting
Solid theoretical grounding: Convergence analysis (Props B.1-B.2), clear explanation of why existing methods fail with few steps, rigorous derivations with bias/variance analysis
Comprehensive experimental validation: 14 tasks across three benchmarks, thorough ablations isolating component contributions, additional validation on toy problems and multi-modal tasks
Strong practical improvements: Inference latency reduced 3-4× vs diffusion baselines (0.46ms vs 0.97-1.68ms); 50% training time reduction while maintaining/exceeding baseline performance
Excellent reproducibility: Detailed hyperparameters, algorithm pseudo-code, implementation details, and promised code availability
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: Core components are from existing work (MeanFlow from Geng et al. 2025; MaxEnt RL from Haarnoja et al. 2018; SNIS/ESS weighting are standard techniques). Contribution is primarily engineering rather than methodological innovation
Still requires 2 sampling steps: 3× slower than one-step policies (SAC/TD3: 0.14-0.15ms vs MFPO: 0.46ms). Framing as 'few-step improvement' is qualified by remaining gap to truly efficient methods

Technical assumptions lack full justification: (1) Prop B.2 assumes K₁,K₂ → ∞ and Boltzmann policy in policy class without discussing practical implications; (2) L2 loss vs KL divergence equivalence (page 7) assumed without rigorous justification; (3) ADN approximation error shown empirically but lacks theoretical bounds

Narrow experimental scope: All tasks are standard continuous control in MuJoCo environments; no vision-based tasks, sparse reward settings, or exploration-critical domains where efficiency gains would matter most; large error bars suggest high variance without significance testing

Incomplete comparisons: Missing comparison with concurrent few-step method Shortcut Models; FlowRL step count comparison complicated by footnote noting 2 forward evaluations per step; no sample efficiency analysis (environment steps to convergence)

Missing technical analyses: No investigation of failure modes or when MFPO underperforms; limited discussion of expressivity limits of MeanFlow vs diffusion policies; SNIS efficiency assumptions (Eq. 24-26) not validated when proposals poorly match target early in training
